title: The FHA 203(k) Process: From Contractor Bid to Final Draw
metaDescription: Step by step through a 203(k) renovation: contractor bids, consultant write-up, appraisal, closing, draw inspections, change orders and the final release.
h1: The FHA 203(k) Renovation Process, Step by Step
dek: A 203(k) renovation moves through a fixed sequence: scope and bids, lender and appraisal review, closing, then construction paid in draws after each stage is inspected. Most friction comes from bids that do not match the scope, unapproved changes and incomplete draw paperwork.
keyTakeaways: Renovation money in a 203(k) is held in an escrow account after closing and released in draws as completed work is verified.
On a Standard 203(k), the 203(k) Consultant writes the scope, reviews bids and inspects work before each draw is released.
Contractor bids must be itemized and match the work write-up or proposed scope line by line.
Any change to the scope needs written approval before the work is done, or it may not be paid from loan funds.
Delays usually come from mismatched bids, missing documents, permit issues and change orders submitted after the fact.

sections.h2: How does the 203(k) process work from start to finish?
sections.body:
An FHA 203(k) renovation follows a sequence that is more structured than a typical cash renovation, because the lender is lending against a house that does not exist yet in its finished form. Every step is designed to make sure the money is spent on the agreed work and that the finished house supports the loan.

The broad sequence looks like this:
- The borrower is prequalified by an FHA-approved lender that originates 203(k) loans, and the lender confirms whether a Standard or Limited 203(k) fits.
- The borrower finds a property and gets it under contract, ideally with enough time in the contract for the 203(k) steps.
- On a Standard 203(k), a 203(k) Consultant inspects the property and prepares a work write-up and cost estimate. On a Limited 203(k), the contractor's itemized proposal usually defines the work, with a consultant involved if the lender requires one.
- Contractors submit itemized bids that match the scope.
- The lender reviews the scope, bids and contractor information and orders an appraisal based on the value of the home after the proposed work is completed.
- The loan closes. Renovation funds go into an escrow or rehabilitation account rather than to the borrower or contractor.
- Construction begins, and the contractor requests draws as stages of work are finished.
- Each draw is inspected and approved before funds are released.
- After the work is complete and passes final inspection, the final draw and any holdback are released.

Understanding that sequence helps every party plan. Most delays come from a step being started before the previous one is finished, or from documents that do not match each other.

sections.h2: Step one: the scope and the contractor bid
sections.body:
Everything in a 203(k) project flows from the scope of work. On a Standard 203(k), the 203(k) Consultant's work write-up is the scope. It lists each repair and improvement, including required items that bring the property up to FHA standards and items the borrower wants, along with the consultant's cost estimate.

The contractor's bid should mirror that document. That means:
- The same line items, in the same order where possible.
- Labor and materials priced for each item, not lumped together.
- Clear specifications for materials and finishes.
- Permit costs identified.
- A start date and an expected completion approach that fits the program's requirements.

A bid that reorganizes the work, combines items or prices work that is not in the write-up forces the consultant and lender to reconcile two documents. That slows underwriting and often produces a round of revisions.

On a Limited 203(k), the contractor's proposal often carries more weight because a consultant may not be involved. That makes clarity even more important. The lender needs to see exactly what will be done and what each item costs, and the lender will check that the work is eligible and nonstructural.

Lenders also review the contractor. Expect to provide a license where the jurisdiction requires one, proof of insurance, references and a signed contractor agreement or acknowledgment specific to the 203(k) program.

Genstone Construction works as an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, and its bids are prepared to follow the write-up line by line. Any contractor bidding 203(k) work should do the same, because a well-matched bid is the single biggest factor in moving the file through underwriting without delay.

sections.h2: Step two: lender review, appraisal and closing
sections.body:
Once the scope and bid are settled, the lender assembles the loan.

The lender reviews the bid against the scope and the consultant's estimate on a Standard loan, checks that all items are eligible, and confirms that required repairs are included. If the bid and the write-up differ significantly, the lender will ask for an explanation or a revision.

The appraisal is ordered on an as-completed basis. The appraiser receives the scope and estimates the value of the property after the proposed improvements are made. That value, along with the purchase price or existing debt, the rehabilitation cost and FHA limits, determines the maximum loan.

On a Standard 203(k), the loan typically includes a contingency reserve to cover unforeseen conditions found during construction, such as damage concealed behind walls. Older homes and properties with visible deferred maintenance may warrant a larger reserve. The loan may also include other costs allowed by the program, such as permit fees, consultant fees and, in some cases, mortgage payments for a period when the home cannot be occupied.

At closing, the purchase or refinance is completed and the renovation funds are placed in an escrow or rehabilitation account managed by the lender. The contractor is not paid at closing, except where the program and lender permit an upfront amount, for example for materials ordered in advance. The rules for upfront payments vary, so the contractor and borrower should confirm them with the lender before closing.

After closing, the clock starts on construction. Program rules and the loan documents set expectations for when work begins and how long it may take.

A draw is a payment from the rehabilitation escrow account to the contractor for work that has been completed. Draws are how the 203(k) program ties payment to progress.

A typical draw follows this pattern:
- The contractor completes a stage of work.
- The contractor, often with the borrower's signature, submits a draw request listing the completed items.
- On a Standard 203(k), the 203(k) Consultant inspects the property and confirms which items are complete. On a Limited 203(k), the lender's inspection process applies.
- The lender reviews the inspection report and the draw request, and may update title to confirm no new liens have been filed.
- Funds are released, typically by a check or transfer that may require both the borrower and contractor to sign or approve.

Draws are usually tied to items on the write-up rather than a schedule. If the consultant confirms that the roof, rough plumbing and electrical service upgrade are complete, the draw can include those items at their bid amounts.

A holdback is commonly withheld from each draw and released at the end of the project, after final inspection and any required lien waivers. This protects the borrower and lender against incomplete work and unpaid subcontractors.

The Standard 203(k) usually allows several draws over the course of a project. The Limited 203(k) uses a simpler disbursement structure with fewer draws. The exact number and timing depend on program rules and the lender's procedures.

For contractors, the practical lesson is that cash flow on a 203(k) follows inspections. Plan stages so each draw request covers a clear group of finished items, and do not start the next stage expecting money that has not been inspected yet.

sections.h2: What role do consultant inspections play?
sections.body:
On a Standard 203(k), the consultant is the person who decides what counts as complete. Understanding how consultants inspect helps borrowers and contractors avoid rejected draws.

Consultants inspect against the write-up. They check each item listed in the draw request and confirm whether it matches the description, specification and quantity in the scope. An item that is mostly done, or done differently than described, may be excluded from the draw or partially credited.

Consultants look for finished work, not effort. A kitchen with cabinets installed but counters on back order is not a finished kitchen item. A bathroom with tile set but no grout may be partially credited at most. Splitting larger items into smaller line items in the original bid helps, because it allows completed parts to be paid without waiting for the whole room.

Consultants also check for health and safety items, required repairs and permit inspections where the jurisdiction requires them. A draw that includes electrical or plumbing work may need evidence that the municipal inspection passed.

They document change orders and confirm that any approved changes are reflected in the work.

The final inspection confirms that every item in the write-up is complete and that the property meets the required standards. It precedes release of the final draw and holdback.

Good practice for contractors is to walk the job with the draw request in hand before calling for an inspection, and to photograph completed items. Good practice for borrowers is to be available to sign draw requests promptly, since a signature delay holds up payment just as much as an incomplete item.

sections.h2: How are change orders handled on a 203(k)?
sections.body:
A change order is any change to the approved scope of work, whether it adds, removes or modifies an item. On a 203(k), change orders follow a formal path because the lender is holding funds against a specific scope.

The usual change order process:
- The need for a change is identified, whether because of a hidden condition, a code requirement or a borrower request.
- The contractor documents the change and prices it, typically with photos for hidden conditions.
- On a Standard 203(k), the consultant reviews and documents the change. The borrower approves it.
- The lender approves the change and determines how it will be funded.
- Only then does the work proceed.

Changes that address unforeseen conditions or required repairs can often be funded from the contingency reserve. Changes the borrower chooses for preference, such as upgrading a finish, may need to be paid separately or offset by removing other items, depending on lender rules and the remaining reserve.

The most common mistake is doing the work first and asking for approval later. An unapproved change may not be paid from the escrow account, which leaves the contractor or the borrower to cover it. Even urgent work, such as stopping an active leak discovered during demolition, should be documented immediately and submitted for approval as soon as possible.

A clear, itemized original scope reduces change orders, because borrowers and contractors agree on exactly what is included before closing. Unit-priced lines for predictable unknowns, such as subfloor replacement or roof decking, also make change orders faster to approve.

sections.h2: Typical friction points, and how to avoid them
sections.body:
Most 203(k) projects that run into trouble hit the same handful of problems.

Bids that do not match the write-up. If line items, quantities or specifications differ, underwriting stalls while documents are reconciled. Bid directly against the write-up.

Missing contractor documents. Licenses, insurance certificates and program-specific agreements requested late hold up closing. Provide them with the bid.

Unrealistic scopes. A scope priced too low may get the loan approved but leave the project short on money. A scope with extras the appraisal cannot support may reduce the loan amount. Price honestly from the start.

Permit delays. If the jurisdiction requires permits, apply as soon as allowed after closing, and build plan review into the start date.

Draw requests for unfinished work. Requests for items that are not complete get reduced or rejected, which costs an inspection trip and time. Request only completed items.

Slow signatures. Borrowers who are hard to reach for draw signatures or change order approvals slow payment and work. Agree on how quickly approvals will happen.

Unapproved changes. Work done outside the approved scope may not be paid from loan funds.

Occupancy conflicts. Living in the home during work can complicate scheduling, utility shutoffs and access. Plan the order of work around the household.

Nearly all of these are solved by preparation: a clear write-up, a matching bid, complete paperwork, permit planning and an agreed communication rhythm between borrower, contractor, consultant and lender.

sections.h2: The final draw and project closeout
sections.body:
The end of a 203(k) project is its own process, and planning for it shortens the time between finishing the work and getting paid.

Before requesting the final draw, the contractor should complete every item in the write-up and the approved change orders, finish the punch list, and clean the property. Any permits should be closed with final inspections passed, and any certificate the jurisdiction issues on completion should be obtained.

The final inspection confirms that all work is complete and meets required standards. On a Standard 203(k), the consultant performs it. The lender may also require a final appraisal update or completion report confirming that the improvements were made as described.

The lender will usually require lien waivers from the contractor and, in many cases, from subcontractors and major suppliers, confirming they have been paid and give up the right to file liens for the work. A title update may confirm no liens were filed.

Once documentation is complete, the lender releases the final draw and the holdback. Any unused contingency reserve is handled according to program rules, which may apply it to the loan balance.

For borrowers, closeout is also the moment to collect warranty information, equipment manuals, paint colors and finish specifications, and contact details for follow-up. A contractor who documents the project throughout, with photos, inspection sign-offs and lien waivers collected as the job proceeds, makes the final draw a formality rather than a scramble.

faqs.q: How long does the 203(k) process take?
faqs.a: It depends on the version, the size of the project, the lender, the consultant's schedule, permit timing in the jurisdiction and how quickly bids and documents come together. Limited 203(k) loans generally move faster because the process is simpler. Standard 203(k) loans take longer because they involve a consultant write-up, more detailed review and more draws. The surest way to shorten the process is to submit an itemized bid that matches the scope with complete contractor documents.

faqs.q: When does the contractor get paid on a 203(k) loan?
faqs.a: The contractor is paid through draws from the rehabilitation escrow account as stages of work are completed and inspected. Some programs and lenders permit an upfront amount at closing, for example for materials, but rules vary. A holdback is commonly withheld from each draw and released after the final inspection and lien waivers. The final draw is released once all work is complete and the required documentation has been received.

faqs.q: What happens if the contractor finds hidden damage during a 203(k)?
faqs.a: The contractor should document the condition with photos and a written change order, and submit it for approval before proceeding, except for true emergencies such as an active leak. On a Standard 203(k), the consultant reviews the change and the borrower and lender approve it. Repairs for unforeseen conditions are often funded from the contingency reserve built into the loan. Work done without approval may not be paid from loan funds.

faqs.q: Who inspects the work before a 203(k) draw is released?
faqs.a: On a Standard 203(k), the FHA-approved 203(k) Consultant inspects the work and confirms which items in the write-up are complete before the lender releases funds. On a Limited 203(k), inspection requirements depend on the project size: an inspection is required for projects over $15,000, and the lender decides for projects of $15,000 or less. Municipal permit inspections are separate and may also be required.

faqs.q: What documents does a 203(k) contractor need to provide?
faqs.a: Lenders commonly ask for an itemized bid matching the scope, a contractor license where the jurisdiction requires one, proof of liability insurance and workers' compensation where applicable, references, and a signed program-specific contractor agreement. During construction, contractors submit draw requests and change orders. At closeout, they provide lien waivers, permit sign-offs and any completion certificates. Having these ready speeds every stage of the process.
